{{Short description|Shape in the geometry of numbers}}
In the [[geometry of numbers]], the '''Klein polyhedron''', named after [[Felix Klein]], is used to generalize the concept of [[simple continued fraction]]s to higher dimensions.

== Definition ==

Let <math>\textstyle C</math> be a closed [[Simplicial complex|simplicial]] [[Cone (linear algebra)|cone]] in [[Euclidean space]] <math>\textstyle \mathbb{R}^n</math>. The ''Klein polyhedron'' of <math>\textstyle C</math> is the [[convex hull]] of the non-zero points of <math>\textstyle C \cap \mathbb{Z}^n</math>.

== Relation to continued fractions ==
[[File:Klein continued fraction.svg|thumb|right|The Klein continued fraction for <math>\textstyle \alpha=\varphi</math> ([[Golden Ratio]]) with the Klein polyhedra encoding the odd terms in blue and the Klein polyhedra encoding the even terms in red.]]
Suppose <math>\textstyle \alpha > 0</math> is an [[irrational number]]. In <math>\textstyle \mathbb{R}^2</math>, the cones generated by <math>\textstyle \{(1, \alpha), (1, 0)\}</math> and by <math>\textstyle \{(1, \alpha), (0, 1)\}</math> give rise to two Klein polyhedra, each of which is bounded by a sequence of adjoining line segments. Define the ''integer length'' of a [[line segment]] to be one less than the size of its intersection with <math>\textstyle \mathbb{Z}^2.</math> Then the [[integer]] lengths of the edges of these two Klein polyhedra encode the continued-fraction expansion of <math>\textstyle \alpha</math>, one matching the even terms and the other matching the odd terms.

== Graphs associated with the Klein polyhedron ==

Suppose <math>\textstyle C</math> is generated by a basis <math>\textstyle (a_i)</math> of <math>\textstyle \mathbb{R}^n</math> (so that <math>\textstyle C = \{ \sum_i \lambda_i a_i : (\forall i) \; \lambda_i \geq 0 \}</math>), and let <math>\textstyle (w_i)</math> be the dual basis (so that <math>\textstyle C = \{ x : (\forall i) \; \langle w_i, x \rangle \geq 0\}</math>). Write <math>\textstyle D(x)</math> for the line generated by the vector <math>\textstyle x</math>, and <math>\textstyle H(x)</math> for the [[hyperplane]] orthogonal to <math>\textstyle x</math>.

Call the vector <math>\textstyle x \in \mathbb{R}^n</math> ''irrational'' if <math>\textstyle H(x) \cap \mathbb{Q}^n = \{0\}</math>; and call the cone <math>\textstyle C</math> irrational if all the vectors <math>\textstyle a_i</math> and <math>\textstyle w_i</math> are irrational.

The boundary <math>\textstyle V</math> of a Klein polyhedron is called a ''sail''. Associated with the sail <math>\textstyle V</math> of an irrational cone are two [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]]:
* the graph <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm e}(V)</math> whose vertices are vertices of <math>\textstyle V</math>, two vertices being joined if they are endpoints of a (one-dimensional) edge of <math>\textstyle V</math>;
* the graph <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm f}(V)</math> whose vertices are <math>\textstyle (n-1)</math>-dimensional faces (''chambers'') of <math>\textstyle V</math>, two chambers being joined if they share an <math>\textstyle (n-2)</math>-dimensional face.

Both of these graphs are structurally related to the directed graph <math>\textstyle \Upsilon_n</math> whose set of vertices is <math>\textstyle \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Q})</math>, where vertex <math>\textstyle A</math> is joined to vertex <math>\textstyle B</math> if and only if <math>\textstyle A^{-1}B</math> is of the form <math>\textstyle UW</math> where

: <math>U = \left( \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & \cdots & 0 & c_1 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 1 & c_{n-1} \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & c_n \end{array} \right)</math>

(with <math>\textstyle c_i \in \mathbb{Q}</math>, <math>\textstyle c_n \neq 0</math>) and <math>\textstyle W</math> is a [[permutation matrix]]. Assuming that <math>\textstyle V</math> has been [[Triangulation (geometry)|triangulated]], the vertices of each of the graphs <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm e}(V)</math> and <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm f}(V)</math> can be described in terms of the graph <math>\textstyle \Upsilon_n</math>:
* Given any path <math>\textstyle (x_0, x_1, \ldots)</math> in <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm e}(V)</math>, one can find a path <math>\textstyle (A_0, A_1, \ldots)</math> in <math>\textstyle \Upsilon_n</math> such that <math>\textstyle x_k = A_k (e)</math>, where <math>\textstyle e</math> is the vector <math>\textstyle (1, \ldots, 1) \in \mathbb{R}^n</math>.
* Given any path <math>\textstyle (\sigma_0, \sigma_1, \ldots)</math> in <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm f}(V)</math>, one can find a path <math>\textstyle (A_0, A_1, \ldots)</math> in <math>\textstyle \Upsilon_n</math> such that <math>\textstyle \sigma_k = A_k (\Delta)</math>, where <math>\textstyle \Delta</math> is the <math>\textstyle (n-1)</math>-dimensional [[Simplex#The standard simplex|standard simplex]] in <math>\textstyle \mathbb{R}^n</math>.

== Generalization of Lagrange's theorem ==

[[Lagrange]] proved that for an irrational real number <math>\textstyle \alpha</math>, the continued-fraction expansion of <math>\textstyle \alpha</math> is [[periodic continued fraction|periodic]] if and only if <math>\textstyle \alpha</math> is a [[quadratic irrational]]. Klein polyhedra allow us to generalize this result.

Let <math>\textstyle K \subseteq \mathbb{R}</math> be a totally real [[algebraic number field]] of degree <math>\textstyle n</math>, and let <math>\textstyle \alpha_i : K \to \mathbb{R}</math> be the <math>\textstyle n</math> real embeddings of <math>\textstyle K</math>. The simplicial cone <math>\textstyle C</math> is said to be ''split'' over <math>\textstyle K</math> if <math>\textstyle C = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : (\forall i) \; \alpha_i(\omega_1) x_1 + \ldots + \alpha_i(\omega_n) x_n \geq 0 \}</math> where <math>\textstyle \omega_1, \ldots, \omega_n</math> is a basis for <math>\textstyle K</math> over <math>\textstyle \mathbb{Q}</math>.

Given a path <math>\textstyle (A_0, A_1, \ldots)</math> in <math>\textstyle \Upsilon_n</math>, let <math>\textstyle R_k = A_{k+1} A_k^{-1}</math>. The path is called ''periodic'', with period <math>\textstyle m</math>, if <math>\textstyle R_{k+qm} = R_k</math> for all <math>\textstyle k, q \geq 0</math>. The ''period matrix'' of such a path is defined to be <math>\textstyle A_m A_0^{-1}</math>. A path in <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm e}(V)</math> or <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm f}(V)</math> associated with such a path is also said to be periodic, with the same period matrix.

The generalized Lagrange theorem states that for an irrational simplicial cone <math>\textstyle C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n</math>, with generators <math>\textstyle (a_i)</math> and <math>\textstyle (w_i)</math> as above and with sail <math>\textstyle V</math>, the following three conditions are equivalent:
* <math>\textstyle C</math> is split over some totally real algebraic number field of degree <math>\textstyle n</math>.
* For each of the <math>\textstyle a_i</math> there is  periodic path of vertices <math>\textstyle x_0, x_1, \ldots</math> in <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm e}(V)</math> such that the <math>\textstyle x_k</math> asymptotically approach the line <math>\textstyle D(a_i)</math>; and the period matrices of these paths all commute.
* For each of the <math>\textstyle w_i</math> there is  periodic path of chambers <math>\textstyle \sigma_0, \sigma_1, \ldots</math> in <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm f}(V)</math> such that the <math>\textstyle \sigma_k</math> asymptotically approach the hyperplane <math>\textstyle H(w_i)</math>; and the period matrices of these paths all commute.

=== Example ===

Take <math>\textstyle n = 2</math> and <math>\textstyle K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})</math>. Then the simplicial cone <math>\textstyle \{(x,y) : x \geq 0, \vert y \vert \leq x / \sqrt{2}\}</math> is split over <math>\textstyle K</math>. The vertices of the sail are the points <math>\textstyle (p_k, \pm q_k)</math> corresponding to the even convergents <math>\textstyle p_k / q_k</math> of the continued fraction for <math>\textstyle \sqrt{2}</math>. The path of vertices <math>\textstyle (x_k)</math> in the positive quadrant starting at <math>\textstyle (1, 0)</math> and proceeding in a positive direction is <math>\textstyle ((1,0), (3,2), (17,12), (99,70), \ldots)</math>. Let <math>\textstyle \sigma_k</math> be the line segment joining <math>\textstyle x_k</math> to <math>\textstyle x_{k+1}</math>. Write <math>\textstyle \bar{x}_k</math> and <math>\textstyle \bar{\sigma}_k</math> for the reflections of <math>\textstyle x_k</math> and <math>\textstyle \sigma_k</math> in the <math>\textstyle x</math>-axis. Let <math>\textstyle T = \left( \begin{array}{cc} 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{array} \right)</math>, so that <math>\textstyle x_{k+1} = T x_k</math>, and let <math>\textstyle R = \left( \begin{array}{cc} 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{cc} 1 & 6 \\ 0 & -1 \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{cc} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{array} \right)</math>.

Let <math>\textstyle M_{\mathrm e} = \left( \begin{array}{cc} \frac12 & \frac12 \\ \frac14 & -\frac14 \end{array} \right)</math>, <math>\textstyle \bar{M}_{\mathrm e} = \left( \begin{array}{cc} \frac12 & \frac12 \\ -\frac14 & \frac14 \end{array} \right)</math>, <math>\textstyle M_{\mathrm f} = \left( \begin{array}{cc} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{array} \right)</math>, and <math>\textstyle \bar{M}_{\mathrm f} = \left( \begin{array}{cc} 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 \end{array} \right)</math>.

* The paths <math>\textstyle (M_{\mathrm e} R^k)</math> and <math>\textstyle (\bar{M}_{\mathrm e} R^k)</math> are periodic (with period one) in <math>\textstyle \Upsilon_2</math>, with period matrices <math>\textstyle M_{\mathrm e} R M_{\mathrm e}^{-1} = T</math> and <math>\textstyle \bar{M}_{\mathrm e} R \bar{M}_{\mathrm e}^{-1} = T^{-1}</math>. We have <math>\textstyle x_k = M_{\mathrm e} R^k (e)</math> and  <math>\textstyle \bar{x}_k = \bar{M}_{\mathrm e} R^k (e)</math>.
* The paths <math>\textstyle (M_{\mathrm f} R^k)</math> and <math>\textstyle (\bar{M}_{\mathrm f} R^k)</math> are periodic (with period one) in <math>\textstyle \Upsilon_2</math>, with period matrices <math>\textstyle M_{\mathrm f} R M_{\mathrm f}^{-1} = T</math> and <math>\textstyle \bar{M}_{\mathrm f} R \bar{M}_{\mathrm f}^{-1} = T^{-1}</math>. We have <math>\textstyle \sigma_k = M_{\mathrm f} R^k (\Delta)</math> and  <math>\textstyle \bar{\sigma}_k = \bar{M}_{\mathrm f} R^k (\Delta)</math>.

== Generalization of approximability ==

A real number <math>\textstyle \alpha > 0</math> is called ''[[Badly approximable number|badly approximable]]'' if <math>\textstyle \{ q (p \alpha - q) : p,q \in \mathbb{Z}, q > 0\}</math> is bounded away from zero. An irrational number is badly approximable [[if and only if]] the partial quotients of its continued fraction are bounded.<ref name=Bug245>{{cite book | last=Bugeaud | first=Yann | title=Distribution modulo one and Diophantine approximation | series=Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics | volume=193 | location=Cambridge | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=2012 | isbn=978-0-521-11169-0 | zbl=1260.11001 | page=245 }}</ref> This fact admits of a generalization in terms of Klein polyhedra.

Given a simplicial cone <math>\textstyle C = \{ x : (\forall i) \; \langle w_i, x \rangle \geq 0\}</math> in <math>\textstyle \mathbb{R}^n</math>, where <math>\textstyle \langle w_i, w_i \rangle = 1</math>, define the ''norm minimum'' of <math>\textstyle C</math> as <math>\textstyle N(C) = \inf \{ \prod_i \langle w_i, x \rangle : x \in \mathbb{Z}^n \cap C \setminus \{0\} \}</math>.

Given vectors <math>\textstyle \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m \in \mathbb{Z}^n</math>, let <math>\textstyle [\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m] = \sum_{i_1 < \cdots < i_n} \vert \det(\mathbf{v}_{i_1} \cdots \mathbf{v}_{i_n}) \vert</math>. This is the Euclidean volume of <math>\textstyle \{ \sum_i \lambda_i \mathbf{v}_i : (\forall i) \; 0 \leq \lambda_i \leq 1 \}</math>.

Let <math>\textstyle V</math> be the sail of an irrational simplicial cone <math>\textstyle C</math>.

* For a vertex <math>\textstyle x</math> of <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm e}(V)</math>, define <math>\textstyle [x] = [\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m]</math> where <math>\textstyle \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m</math> are primitive vectors in <math>\textstyle \mathbb{Z}^n</math> generating the edges emanating from <math>\textstyle x</math>.
* For a vertex <math>\textstyle \sigma</math> of <math>\textstyle \Gamma_{\mathrm f}(V)</math>, define <math>\textstyle [\sigma] = [\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m]</math> where <math>\textstyle \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m</math> are the extreme points of <math>\textstyle \sigma</math>.

Then <math>\textstyle N(C) > 0</math> if and only if <math>\textstyle \{ [x] : x \in \Gamma_{\mathrm e}(V) \}</math> and <math>\textstyle \{ [\sigma] : \sigma \in \Gamma_{\mathrm f}(V) \}</math> are both bounded.

The quantities <math>\textstyle [x]</math> and <math>\textstyle [\sigma]</math> are called ''determinants''. In two dimensions, with the cone generated by <math>\textstyle \{(1, \alpha), (1,0)\}</math>, they are just the partial quotients of the continued fraction of <math>\textstyle \alpha</math>.
